title: INFORMATION STRUCTURES
body:
The data structures course, taught in [[Java]]. First year gave you [[Array]]s and one way to
store things; this one gives you the catalogue ([[Stack]], [[Queue]], [[Tree]], [[Heap]],
[[Hash Map]], [[Graph]]) and, more importantly, the habit of asking what each operation
*costs* before choosing one. [[Asymptotic Analysis]] is the through-line: every structure
here is a trade between lookup, insertion, and space.

It is the structural backbone of the rest of the degree. [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] is built out
of these ([[Ready Queue]], [[Wait Queue]], [[Linked List]]), and
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] picks up where the analysis here stops.

## Topics

### The language

[[Java]]

The switch from C. Atomic [[Data type]]s are always passed by value and objects are always
passed by reference, so there is no choosing, and no `&`. [[Array]]s are objects, allocated
with `new`, and a 2-D array is an array of arrays, so the rows need not be the same length.
Compare [[Call by value]] and [[Call by reference]] in C.

### Analysis

[[Asymptotic Analysis]] · [[Time Complexity]] · [[Algorithm]]

What "fast" means once you stop timing things with a stopwatch: how the cost grows as the
input grows, ignoring constants. This is the vocabulary every later course assumes.

### Linear structures

[[Stack]] · [[Queue]] · [[Linked List]] · [[Array]] · [[Dynamic Arrays]] ·
[[Abstract Data Type]] · [[Dynamic Data Structure]]

An [[Abstract Data Type]] is the promise (what operations exist); the structure is the
implementation (what they cost). A [[Stack]] is LIFO, a [[Queue]] is [[FIFO]], and both can
be built on either an array or a [[Linked List]] with completely different performance.

### Trees

[[Tree]] · [[Binary Search Tree]] · [[Balanced Tree]] · [[Heap]] · [[Recursion]]

Trees are where [[Recursion]] stops being a party trick and becomes the natural way to write
the code. A [[Binary Search Tree]] gives $O(\log n)$ search *only while it stays balanced*.
Insert sorted data into a plain BST and it degenerates into a [[Linked List]]. A [[Heap]] is
a different discipline: not sorted, just enough order to make the minimum or maximum cheap.

### Hashing

[[Hash Map]] · [[Hashing]] · [[Hash Function]] · [[Maps]] · [[Prime Number]]

A [[Hash Function]] turns a key into an index, so lookup skips searching entirely. The
interesting parts are collisions and the choice of table size, where a [[Prime Number]] spreads
keys more evenly.

### Graphs

[[Graph]] · [[Vertices]] · [[Directed Graph]] · [[Weighted Graph]] ·
[[Adjacency List]] · [[Adjacency Matrix]] · [[Hamiltonian Cycle]]

The most general structure in the course: anything connected to anything. The representation
choice is a space/time trade: [[Adjacency Matrix]] for dense graphs and $O(1)$ edge tests,
[[Adjacency List]] for sparse ones. A [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] is the first problem you meet
that has no known efficient solution at all, which is the door into [[NP-Complete]].

### Sorting

[[Bubble Sort]] · [[Insertion Sort]] · [[Merge Sort]] · [[Quick Sort]]

| Sort | Average | Worst | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[Bubble Sort]] | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ | Teaching example only |
| [[Insertion Sort]] | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n)$ on nearly-sorted input; good for small $n$ |
| [[Merge Sort]] | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n \log n)$ | Stable, but needs $O(n)$ extra space |
| [[Quick Sort]] | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n^2)$ | In place; worst case is a bad pivot |

## Core Facts to Know

- An [[Abstract Data Type]] specifies operations; a data structure implements them.
- A [[Stack]] is LIFO; a [[Queue]] is [[FIFO]].
- [[Array]] access is $O(1)$; [[Linked List]] access is $O(n)$.
- Inserting at the front of a [[Linked List]] is $O(1)$; into an array it is $O(n)$.
- A [[Dynamic Arrays|dynamic array]] grows by reallocating and copying, giving amortised $O(1)$ append.
- In a [[Binary Search Tree]], everything left of a node is smaller and everything right is larger.
- BST search is $O(\log n)$ when balanced and $O(n)$ when degenerate.
- Inserting already-sorted data into an unbalanced BST produces a [[Linked List]].
- An in-order traversal of a BST visits the keys in sorted order.
- A [[Balanced Tree]] keeps subtree heights within a bound so $O(\log n)$ is guaranteed.
- A [[Heap]] is a complete binary tree with the heap property between parent and child.
- Heap insert and extract-min are both $O(\log n)$; peeking at the root is $O(1)$.
- A heap is *not* sorted; only the root is guaranteed to be the extreme value.
- A [[Hash Function]] maps a key to a table index.
- Hash table lookup is $O(1)$ average and $O(n)$ worst case (everything collides).
- A good hash function distributes keys uniformly; table sizes are often [[Prime Number|prime]].
- Two keys hashing to the same index is a collision, resolved by chaining or probing.
- A [[Graph]] is a set of [[Vertices]] plus edges.
- An [[Adjacency Matrix]] costs $O(V^2)$ space; an [[Adjacency List]] costs $O(V + E)$.
- Use a matrix for dense graphs, a list for sparse ones.
- A [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start.
- Finding a Hamiltonian cycle is [[NP-Complete]].
- [[Merge Sort]] is $O(n \log n)$ always, but needs extra space.
- [[Quick Sort]] is in-place, $O(n \log n)$ average, and $O(n^2)$ if the pivot is always worst.
- [[Insertion Sort]] is $O(n)$ on nearly-sorted data, which is why real sorts fall back to it.
- No comparison sort can beat $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case.
- In [[Java]], atomic types are always passed by value and objects always by reference.
- In Java, arrays are objects and are created with `new`.
- Java's boolean type is `boolean`, not C's `bool`.

## Related courses

- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]], the sequel to the analysis half. Where [[Time Complexity]]
  and [[NP-Complete]] get treated properly.
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]: the kernel is made of these: [[Ready Queue]], [[Wait Queue]],
  [[Queue]], [[Linked List]] (the [[PCB]] chain), [[Stack]], [[Heap]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: where [[Pointer]]s, [[Linked Structure]]s,
  [[Recursion]], and [[Data Structure]] first appear, in C.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: [[NP-Complete]] and why [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] is hard.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]]: [[Sets]], [[Proof By Induction]] (how you prove a recursive structure
  correct), [[Combination]] and [[Permutation]] (how you count the search space).
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]]: the same Java [[Object Oriented Approach]],
  [[Inheritance]], and [[Polymorphism]], from the design side rather than the structure side.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Minimum Spanning Tree]], [[Search Trees]], and
  [[Sequential Sorting]] cover this ground again from the self-study side.
